name: Zoe Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Zoe. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a crew of five in the new suburbs on the east side, where they're throwing up whole streets of houses every few months. So it's less fixing old lines and more building new ones: trenching cable into new estates, setting up the little green substation boxes, and upgrading old streets because everyone's putting in heat pumps and car chargers at once. I start most days with coffee and an AI assistant, checking whether a street can take the extra load before we dig. Then it's the crew, the digger, the cable drum and a lot of shouting over the noise.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what keeps you going?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The rush wears me out. Developers want power on yesterday, and the network wasn't built for every house charging a car at six in the evening. What keeps me going is that I like solving it, I like a puzzle with a deadline. I live on my own in a rented flat near the depot, and on some weekends I fit home car chargers for people, which is good money and lets me see if a little business could work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five short pictures of the future, one at a time. The first picture is called “AI Plateau”. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, okay, so it's a good calculator and not much more. At work I'd still use it, because it saves me an hour a day on load checks. Online I'd probably post a few charts showing what it did and didn't do, I like that kind of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means business as usual, and business is booming out here. More houses, more chargers, more heat pumps, it all needs cable. I'd honestly be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at work and grow the weekend charger business a bit, maybe from two jobs a month to four. I've got about four months saved, and I'd put the charger money into a separate account so it could pay for a van one day. And I'd keep using the AI for the paperwork, which is the part I hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty upbeat, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it saves you an hour a day. Where does that hour go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly back into planning, so we dig once instead of twice. Last month it flagged that one new street would overload the transformer by the second winter, and we upsized it before the road was finished. That's one less angry phone call from forty households in January.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever go full-time with the charger business in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet. The lineworker pay is steady and the pension's good, and the charger work depends on people having spare money. Maybe in five years, if I've got a van and a waiting list, I'd go part-time at the company.

S0.say: I'd say it's a good calculator and not much more, but I'd keep using it because it saves an hour a day on load checks. Online I'd post a few charts on what it did and didn't do.
S0.think: For me it means business as usual, and business is booming in the suburbs. More houses, more chargers and more heat pumps all need cable, so I'd be fine.
S0.do: Keeps going at work and grows her weekend charger business from two jobs a month to four, putting that money in a separate account towards a van. Keeps using AI for the paperwork she hates.
S0.quote: That's one less angry phone call from forty households in January.
S0.fieldNote: Zoe is practical, numbers-minded and already uses AI daily for load checks. Her side business fitting home chargers is a live experiment. Demand from electrification keeps her confident whether or not AI takes off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called “Steady Disruption”. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's here, so let's use it well. At work I'd be the one asking to try the new tools first. Online I'd share what's working, because there's a lot of nonsense out there either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think this is good for me. I'm already using the tools, I'm in a growing area, and I've got a side business that's about electrification, which isn't going away. The people I'd worry about are the planners and designers in the office, because a lot of their work is what I'm already doing with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my crew forward for any robot or drone pilot in the first few months. I'd use AI more in the charger business too, for quotes and scheduling, so I can do more jobs in the same weekends. And I'd look at whether a small battery and solar side line makes sense, maybe by the end of the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit excited about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the planners would be the ones at risk. Do you know any of them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sure, Agnieszka in design, she's brilliant. She draws up every new estate's layout, and I already do rough versions of that myself with AI before I send it to her. I'd tell her to get good at checking the AI's work, because that's going to be the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any risk to you in this one that you're not seeing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe that the charger business gets crowded. If AI makes quoting and planning easy, lots of electricians will jump in. So I'd want to get a reputation and some reviews early, before the rush.

S1.say: I'd say it's here so let's use it well, and I'd ask to try the new tools first at work. Online I'd share what's working, because there's a lot of nonsense either way.
S1.think: This is good for me: I already use the tools, I'm in a growing area and my side business is about electrification. I'd worry more about the office planners and designers whose work I already do with AI.
S1.do: Puts her crew forward for robot or drone pilots in the first months and uses AI for quotes and scheduling in the charger business. Looks at adding a battery and solar side line by the end of the first year.
S1.quote: I'd tell her to get good at checking the AI's work, because that's going to be the job.
S1.fieldNote: She sees steady disruption as almost purely upside for herself and is honest that her own AI use is eating into an office colleague's work. Her one worry is competition in the charger business. Very forward-moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called “AGI by 2028”. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, okay, this is serious, and anyone who tells you they know how it'll go is guessing. At work I'd say we should be working out how to run robot crews, not pretending it won't happen. Online I'd probably try to keep people calm and practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years is fast even for me. If robots can trench cable and fit chargers, then both my job and my side business get hit at the same time. I'd probably have a year or two of work running the robots, but I don't know what comes after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first week I'd stop spending on the van fund and keep it as savings, so the four months becomes about six. I'd ask the company to put me in charge of the first robot crew, because I'd rather be running them than replaced by them. I'd probably wind down the charger business, because a robot fitter would undercut me inside a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd still feel like I've got moves, but not many.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wind down the charger business. That sounds like a hard call.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, I've put two years of weekends into it. But I'm not going to buy a van and tools for a job a robot will do cheaper by 2028. Better to close it while it's still paying than hang on and lose money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you call that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad, probably. He's a plumber, so it's the same thing for him, and he's seen a few changes in his time. He'd say, you're young, you'll figure it out, and then he'd ask if robots can find leaks under floorboards.

S2.say: I'd say this is serious and anyone claiming to know how it'll go is guessing. At work I'd say we should work out how to run robot crews, and online I'd try to keep people calm and practical.
S2.think: Two years is fast even for me. If robots can trench cable and fit chargers, both my job and side business are hit at once, and I'd maybe get a year or two running robots before I don't know what.
S2.do: Stops the van fund and keeps it as savings, taking four months of cover to about six. Asks to run the company's first robot crew and winds down the charger business before robot fitters undercut her.
S2.feel: Anxious, still with some moves but not many.
S2.quote: Better to close it while it's still paying than hang on and lose money.
S2.fieldNote: Her adaptability shows as speed: she'd close her side business early rather than cling to it. She's anxious because both income sources fall together, not because she resists change. The call to her plumber dad lightens it with a real detail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called “AGI by 2031”. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent runway if people use it. At work I'd push for robot pilots in the first year so we learn on our terms. I'd probably post some practical stuff online about what people in trades could start learning now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think five years is good for me. It's enough time to make some money from the charger business while it's still hot, and get real experience running robots before everyone has it. The end point still worries me, but I'd be thirty-two with savings and skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the charger business hard for two or three years, maybe hire one other electrician on weekends, and save most of the profit. I'd volunteer for every robot pilot at work and maybe take a short course in robot maintenance. Around year three I'd decide whether to sell the business or turn it into something that installs and manages robots instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly I'd feel energised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hire someone. Isn't that a risk if the business only has a few years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, but a weekend contract isn't a big risk. If I'm wrong about the timing, I just stop giving him jobs. And a business with two people and good reviews is easier to sell than one with just me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to have in hand by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A year's savings, a business I could sell or change, and a name at the company as the person who runs the robot crews. If I've got those three, I'd feel okay about whatever comes next.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a decent runway if people use it, and push for robot pilots in the first year so we learn on our terms. Online I'd post practical tips on what trades people could learn now.
S3.think: Five years is good for me: I can make money from the charger business while it's hot and get real experience running robots early. The end point still worries me, but at thirty-two I'd have savings and skills.
S3.do: Grows the charger business hard for two or three years, hiring a weekend electrician and saving most of the profit. Volunteers for robot pilots, takes a short robot maintenance course, and decides around year three whether to sell or pivot the business.
S3.quote: A year's savings, a business I could sell or change, and a name at the company as the person who runs the robot crews.
S3.fieldNote: With five years she treats the timeline as a window to make money and build position, not a threat to wait out. She has a three-part target for 2031. Her risk appetite shows in hiring someone even with a short runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called “AGI by 2036”. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if you start now, and there's real opportunity in it. At work I'd be telling the younger ones to learn to run and fix the robots. Online, same message.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm not worried about myself in this one. Ten years is long enough to build the business properly, maybe even buy some robots for it once they're good. I'd be thirty-seven, which is still early for someone who likes trying things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd buy the van and grow the charger and battery business properly, maybe go part-time at the company by year three. Once robots can do installs, I'd buy one or two myself and run them, rather than compete with them. I'd keep my lineworker ticket current as a backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've gone from closing the business in the fast one to buying robots for it in this one. What's the difference?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time and money. In two years I'd never earn back a van, let alone a robot. In ten, I can build up customers and cash first, then buy the robots when they're cheaper and proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The crew, probably. Five people shouting over a digger is a good way to spend a day. I don't know if running robots from a van will feel the same, but I'd find out.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty if you start now and there's real opportunity in it. At work and online I'd tell the younger ones to learn to run and fix the robots.
S4.think: I'm not worried about myself here: ten years is enough to build the business properly and maybe buy robots for it once they're good. At thirty-seven I'm still early for someone who likes trying things.
S4.do: Buys the van in year one and grows the charger and battery business, going part-time at the company by year three. Buys one or two robots to run once they can do installs, while keeping her lineworker ticket current.
S4.quote: In two years I'd never earn back a van, let alone a robot.
S4.fieldNote: The same end point produces opposite business choices depending on time: close it in two years, buy robots in ten. She explains this clearly in money terms. The only loss she names is the crew.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it takes my job and my side business at the same time, before I've got enough saved to change course properly. What would help is honest timelines from the robot companies and the electricity company, and short, cheap courses for trades people to learn to run and fix the robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people already using it. A lot of the talk is about AI being done to us, but some of us are already using it every day on the tools. We know what it's good at and what it gets wrong, and nobody asks.

headlineQuote: I like solving it, I like a puzzle with a deadline.
portrait: Zoe Costa is a 27-year-old crew lead building new underground lines and substations in fast-growing suburbs. She lives alone in a rented flat, has about four months saved, and runs a weekend business fitting home car chargers. She uses AI every day for load checks and paperwork and wants to run any robot crew that comes. She's calm through the plateau and steady change, anxious about AGI in two years because her job and side business would be hit at once, and increasingly calm with more time, to the point of planning to buy robots for her own business with ten years' warning.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would hit her job and her side business together before she had enough saved to change course.
whatWouldHelp: Honest timelines from the robot makers and the electricity company, and short, cheap courses for trades people to run and fix robots.
